# Handle playback errors

Display playback failures, report them, and choose a useful recovery action.

Display playback failures instead of leaving a dead player, report the failure when you need diagnostics, and give users a useful next step.

> **Note**
>
> Using a pre-built [skin](./skins.md)? It already includes the controls shown here. You may still need the media or player setup in this guide. The component examples are for building your own player UI from individual [components](./ui-components.md).

## Recommended approach

Render an [ErrorDialog](../reference/components/error-dialog.md) inside the player container. It reads error state, presents the failure, and dismisses cleanly. The packaged skins include one.

```tsx
import { Container, ErrorDialog } from '@videojs/react';
import { Video, VideoPlayer } from '@videojs/react/video';

export default function App() {
  return (
    <VideoPlayer>
      <Container>
        <Video src="https://stream.mux.com/BV3YZtogl89mg9VcNBhhnHm02Y34zI1nlMuMQfAbl3dM/highest.mp4" muted playsInline />

        <ErrorDialog.Root>
          <ErrorDialog.Popup className="media-error">
            <ErrorDialog.Title />
            <ErrorDialog.Description />
            <ErrorDialog.Close>Dismiss</ErrorDialog.Close>
          </ErrorDialog.Popup>
        </ErrorDialog.Root>
      </Container>
    </VideoPlayer>
  );
}
```

## How it works

The [error feature](../reference/api/feature-error.md) mirrors the media component’s error into player state:

- `error` holds the media’s error — `code`, `message` — or `null` when there is none.
- `dismissError()` clears the error from player state (the media component keeps its own error until a new load).
- Loading a new source resets `error` to `null` automatically.

The dialog owns presentation, not recovery. Decide the next step in your application: let the user dismiss the message, choose another item, refresh an expired URL, or contact support.

## Availability and constraints

- For a terminal failure, load a new or refreshed source to recover. An aborted load or an adapter-specific error may have different behavior.
- Standard media error codes distinguish broad classes — aborted, network, decode, and source-not-supported — rather than root causes. A media adapter can report its own numeric code too.
- Streaming engines handle recoverable segment and network failures before surfacing a terminal error. Do not layer a generic same-source retry loop on top of the engine.
- The feature records `error` events after attachment. An error already present on the media is not copied into state. Keep the error surface mounted regardless of playback state.

Server-rendered `<Video src={...}>` can start loading before hydration and player attachment. To capture startup failures, assign the source only after attachment. Alternatively, after attachment, check the native video’s `error` once through a ref and show an application message if it is already set.

## Common variations

### Offer an application-specific next step

Use the error code and your product context to choose the action. A live event can link to its status page, an authenticated app can refresh an expired playback URL, and a playlist can offer the next item. Keep that action outside `ErrorDialog`; the dialog can close after your application has handled the error.

### Report errors to monitoring

Subscribe to error state and forward new errors to your monitoring service with the source URL and `error.code`. A media error does not automatically appear in JavaScript exception monitoring.

Place a reporter inside `VideoPlayer`, alongside the skin or your custom controls:

```tsx
import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { selectError, usePlayer } from '@videojs/react';

function PlaybackErrorReporter({
  onError,
}: {
  onError: (error: { code: number; message: string }) => void;
}) {
  const error = usePlayer(selectError)?.error;

  useEffect(() => {
    if (error) onError(error);
  }, [error, onError]);

  return null;
}
```

Pass a stable `onError` function that sends the error and current source URL to your monitoring service. The effect runs when the error value changes, not on every player state update.

### Diagnose a reported failure

Start with `error.code` and the affected source URL. Check the browser’s network panel for failed media requests, response status, redirects, CORS headers, and expired credentials. If requests succeed, check the file’s container and codecs against the chosen media component. For HLS or DASH, inspect the streaming engine’s diagnostics for segment and manifest failures; the player error often names only the final outcome.

## Troubleshooting

### The player is black and silent with no error

Not every dead player is a media error — autoplay blocking and an unset source produce no error. Check `error`, `source`, and `paused` in player state to tell them apart. If `play()` rejects with `NotAllowedError`, see [Autoplay](./autoplay.md).

### A `VJS8_LEGACY_*` exception appears

These codes identify Video.js 8 APIs used with the Video.js 10 `video.js` package. Look up the code in the [error code reference](../reference/api/error-codes.md) for its trigger and v10 equivalent. These exceptions are separate from the player’s `error` state, which receives media playback errors after setup.

### Error code says the source isn’t supported

The browser can’t play the format through this media component. HLS in a plain video element outside Safari is the classic case; use the matching streaming media component. See [Media sources](./media-sources.md).

### Reopening the source produces the same error

The failure is probably permanent for that source, such as a 404, revoked token, unsupported codec, or CORS response. Fix or replace the source instead of repeatedly loading the same URL.
